body:
After it was discussed in the core meeting to potentially migrate the `#error` logic to an implementation file, I dig more digging into the potential costs of compile-time constants. I ended up testing two dummy `.cpp` files: one with no includes whatsoever, and one with a single include which includes n number of `static_assert` calls. Here's the outputs as traced by `--debug=action-timestamps`:

### n = 1,000
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.322485 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.090602 seconds

Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.215855 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.218480 seconds

Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 0.797861 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 0.792867 seconds

### n = 10,000
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.416890 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.204370 seconds

Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.193312 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.206657 seconds

Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 0.797588 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 0.785399 seconds

### n = 100,000
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.274416 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.006017 seconds

Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.414354 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.511541 seconds

Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 0.794821 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 0.964146 seconds

### n = 1,000,000
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.333167 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 2.351364 seconds

Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 0.870015 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 1.830625 seconds

Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy1.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 0.838121 seconds
Command execution time: bin\obj\main\dummy2.windows.editor.dev.x86_64.obj: 2.550997 seconds

---

So quite a lot of variance! Both 1k and 10k resulted in functionally identical times, and 100k only slightly pushed compile time out of standard deviation. It only truly had a measurable impact when using a comically excessive 1 million static assertions, bumping up compile times by about a second. This isn't hard-science—SCons is unwieldy at the best of times—but this is enough for me to say that we shouldn't worry about the cost of compile-time constants. Unless we're doing something that adds over 10k compile-time checks in a header that's included everywhere, the results appear truly negligible

This is all to say that I'm gonna keep the `#error` checks in `typedefs.h` :)
